messages.author: c6ca7877bef91eef
messages.subject: Re: Is it possible in ggplot2 to create a combined boxplot and kernel density estimate
parts:
Here is a short function that would help you achieve this. It is a
quick hack and there might be more elegant ways to do this with lesser
lines of code. Let me know if this works.

foo <- function(x){

require(ggplot2);
df1 = data.frame(x = density(x)$x, y = density(x)$y);
df2 = data.frame(t(boxplot.stats(x)$stats));
names(df2) = c('xmin', 'fq', 'med', 'tq', 'xmax');
df = data.frame(df1, df2);

p0 = ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
geom_line() +
geom_errorbarh(aes(x = 0, xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, y = max(df
$y)/2), height = 0.05) +
geom_linerange(aes(x = med, ymin = 0, ymax = y)) +
geom_area(subset = .(x > df$fq[1] & x < df$tq[1]), fill =
'green', alpha = 0.5)

}

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Is it possible in ggplot2 to create a combined boxplot and kernel density estimate
parts:
Hi:

The main problem with RV's function was that the plot was never printed. However, grabbing the data from density() and boxplot.stats() was inspired - nice job. I rewrote the plot part of the function and added several intermediate statistics to make some of the segment locations a little more precise. I hope this works...


kdeBxp <- function(x){

 require(ggplot2)
 # Data frame for generating the kernel density
df1 = data.frame(x = density(x)$x, y = density(x)$y)
# Data frame for holding the boxplot statistics

df2 = data.frame(t(boxplot.stats(x)$stats))
 names(df2) = c('xmin', 'fq', 'med', 'tq', 'xmax')

df2$ymx <- max(df1$y)     # maximum density value
 df2$ymid <- df2$ymx/2     # midpoint of the densities

# Find observed point closest to median and its corresponding y value in df1,
# put in new data frame df3 - this is used to get the vertical segment
  u <- which.min(abs(df1$x - median(df1$x)))
  df3 <- data.frame(x = df1$x[u], y = df1$y[u])

# Determine endpoints of the horizontal whiskers:
df2$iqr <- with(df2, tq - fq)
df2$wmin <- with(df2, max(xmin, fq - 1.5 * iqr))
df2$wmax <- with(df2, min(xmax, tq + 1.5 * iqr))

 p0 <- ggplot() + geom_line(data = df1, aes(x, y), size = 1, color = 'blue') +
    # vertical segment at the median
             geom_segment(data = df3, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = x, yend = 0)) +
    # left and right segments, respectively
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = wmin, y = ymid,
                              xend = fq, yend = ymid)) +
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = tq, y = ymid,
                              xend = wmax, yend = ymid)) +
    # vertical whiskers - reset 0.02 to change height
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = xmin, y = ymid - 0.02,
                                          xend = xmin, yend = ymid + 0.02)) +
             geom_segment(data = df2, aes(x = xmax, y = ymid - 0.02,
                                          xend = xmax, yend = ymid + 0.02)) +
    # filled 'box'
             geom_ribbon(data = subset(df1, x >= df2$fq & x <= df2$tq),
                             aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = y), fill = 'green', alpha = 0.4) +
    # bells and whistles
             theme_bw() + opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
                               panel.grid.minor = theme_blank()) +
             geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), color = 'gray90')

 print(p0)
 invisible()

}

# Example:
kdeBxp(rnorm(100))

Dennis

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Is it possible in ggplot2 to create a combined boxplot and kernel density estimate
parts:
This is one way, but one can fiddle with the details to get what one wants...

df <- data.frame(gp = 1, x = rnorm(100))
g <- ggplot(df)
p1 <- g + geom_density(aes(x = x), fill = 'green', alpha = 0.4) + theme_bw() +
          xlim(-3, 3) + xlab("")
# Some of the options used below are to ensure that the scale of x is the same
# in both the density plot and the box plot
p2 <- g + geom_boxplot(aes(x = gp, y = x), fill = 'orange') + theme_bw() + ylim(-3, 3)  +
        opts(axis.text.y = theme_text(colour = 'white'),
             axis.title.y = theme_text(colour = 'white'),
             panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
             panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(),
             axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
             panel.border = theme_blank(),
             axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
             axis.text.x = theme_blank()) +
        coord_flip()

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(20, 1)))

vplayout <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)
print(p1, vp = vplayout(1:18, 1))
print(p2, vp = vplayout(18:20, 1))

Some comments:
(1) I needed to create a phony grouping variable to get ggplot2 to plot a single boxplot,
     which is why gp has one value in the input data frame df.
(2) I used a large number of rows in the layout argument of viewport to have finer
     control over placement of the two graphs. There are other, probably better ways to go about this.
(3) If the code from grid.newpage() down is not familiar, it is taken out of p. 154 of Hadley's
     book. Another viable option would be to use the gridExtra package for this task.

Dennis

Hi,

There's currently a danger in this approach, which is that the two x
axes may not be well aligned. Consider this,

p1 = p1 + ylab("verrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrry long axis title") +
opts(axis.title.y=theme_text())

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(20, 1)))

vplayout <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)
print(p1, vp = vplayout(1:18, 1))
print(p2, vp = vplayout(18:20, 1))

If possible, facetting would be the best option. Other than that one would want,

- to calculate the width of the y axis label and of the optional
legend (see align.plots() in ggExtra)

or perhaps more easily

- to add a phantom() y axis label for the second graph

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Is it possible in ggplot2 to create a combined boxplot and kernel density estimate
parts:
I agree, Baptiste; if you look at the first two opts of the boxplot p2, I didn't get rid of the text or axis labels on what ended up being the y-axis of the rotated box plot - I simply 'painted' them white to match the background color. Getting rid of them would have distorted the scales on the two panels. Another concern would have been if the value of the grouping variable were different from the order of magnitude of the input vector - e.g., 1 for the group and 10xy for the values of the input vector - that would misalign the scales as well. The user would have to 'know' to substitute a value for the grouping variable in the box plot that was the same order of magnitude as the maximum response, or at least that of the largest label in the main plot.  My purpose was to show that it *could* be done, but I wouldn't write up what I did as a 'ready for production' function for the reasons you mentioned as well as the above. Dealing with where to put the x-axis labels was another headache...

A function to create a density/histogram + boxplot could overcome some of these issues - e.g., one could hard code the titles, to check the order of magnitude of the input vector and generate the grouping variable value accordingly, but these patches highlight the central problem - a more automatic way is needed to ensure that the horizontal scale of the two graphs align properly when rendered on the graphics device. In this situation, I'd be more comfortable writing such a function in base or grid graphics, since one would then have more control over the placement of the two graphics in question and could perform tests on each to ensure that both plots have the same horizontal scale.

Thanks for the appropriate warning...
Dennis

Hi,

There's currently a danger in this approach, which is that the two x
axes may not be well aligned. Consider this,

p1 = p1 + ylab("verrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrry long axis title") +
opts(axis.title.y=theme_text())

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(20, 1)))

vplayout <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)
print(p1, vp = vplayout(1:18, 1))
print(p2, vp = vplayout(18:20, 1))

If possible, facetting would be the best option. Other than that one would want,

- to calculate the width of the y axis label and of the optional
legend (see align.plots() in ggExtra)

or perhaps more easily

- to add a phantom() y axis label for the second graph
